::: {.lead}
*Night Owl Games* has the script of the opening scene of *Rooftop Rescue*
(Lecture 4). Before the artists build the flooded street, the team wants to
**see** the scene: what the camera shows first, how close it comes to
Salma, and how one shot follows another. So they draw a **storyboard**: a
row of simple pictures, one for each shot. In this lesson you plan the
pictures of a scene. Every section ends with a short task.
:::

## Key terms

{{< glossary storyboard panel panel-caption shot wide-shot medium-shot close-up camera-angle composition rule-of-thirds lead-room story-beat screen-direction >}}

## 5.1 See the scene before you build it: the storyboard

Building one shot of a 3D cutscene can take a team days. If the shot is
wrong, the work is lost. A drawing takes two minutes. So the team draws
first (@fig-board).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 5.1 — Storyboard"}
A **storyboard** is a series of simple drawings, called **panels**. Each
panel shows one shot of a scene. Under each panel, a **caption** gives the
shot size, the action or the line, the sound and the time.
:::

![A storyboard of the opening of *Rooftop Rescue*: four panels, each with its notes.](images/storyboard-page.png){#fig-board width=96%}

A panel is small and fast. It has a number, a frame of the screen's shape
(16:9), simple shapes, and **arrows** for movement (@fig-panel). Stick
figures are fine. The board answers three questions: what does the player
see, what happens, and how long does it take?

![The parts of a panel.](images/panel-anatomy.png){#fig-panel width=90%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 5.1 — From script to panels"}
The script says: "EXT. FLOODED STREET – DUSK. Nour jumps into the boat.
NOUR: Hold on, everyone."

1. Panel 1 shows the place. Caption: "Wide: the street at dusk. SFX: water,
   wind. 3 s."
2. Panel 2 shows the action. Caption: "Medium: Nour jumps into the boat.
   SFX: splash. 2 s."
3. Panel 3 shows the line. Caption: "Close-up: Nour. NOUR: Hold on,
   everyone. 2 s."
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Drawing beautiful panels. A storyboard is a plan, not the final art. If one
panel takes twenty minutes, nobody wants to change it. Use simple shapes.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Three panels on paper"}
Fold an A4 paper twice to get four boxes. Use three of them.

1. Draw the three panels of Example 5.1 with simple shapes.
2. Under each panel, write the shot size, the action or the line, a sound
   and a time.

*Your result:* three panels with captions.

::: {.check}
Panel 1: a long water line and houses (wide), "SFX: water, wind. 3 s".
Panel 2: a boat and a stick figure jumping in (medium), "SFX: splash. 2 s".
Panel 3: a big face (close-up), "NOUR: Hold on, everyone. 2 s". Each panel
has a number and a full caption.
:::
:::

## 5.2 How close is the camera? Shot sizes

The same moment can be shown from far or from near. Each **shot size**
tells the player something different (@fig-sizes).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 5.2 — Shot sizes"}
A **wide shot** shows the whole place, with small characters in it. The
first wide shot of a scene is the **establishing shot**. A **medium shot**
shows a character from about the waist up. A **close-up** fills the frame
with a face or one object.
:::

![Three shot sizes: the wide shot answers "where?", the medium shot "what?", the close-up "how does it feel?".](images/shot-sizes.png){#fig-sizes width=96%}

| Shot size | What the player learns | Rooftop Rescue |
|---|---|---|
| Wide (establishing) | where the scene happens | the flooded street at dusk |
| Medium | what a character does | Nour rows the boat |
| Close-up | what a character feels, or a detail | Salma's fear; the cat |

: Shot sizes and what they show. {#tbl-sizes}

The **camera angle** changes the feeling too. From above (a high angle), a
character looks small and weak. From below (a low angle), it looks big and
strong.

::: {.callout-note title="Example 5.2 — A size for each moment"}
1. The scene starts, and the player does not know the place: **wide shot**.
2. Nour rows hard against the water, an action: **medium shot**.
3. Salma says "I won't leave without my cat." The line is about fear:
   **close-up**.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Using the same size for every panel. A board of only medium shots never
shows the place and never shows a feeling. Change the size when the purpose
changes.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Three sizes with your phone"}
Choose one object on your desk (a bottle, a bag).

1. With your phone camera, take a wide shot, a medium shot and a close-up.
2. Under each photo, write what the player would learn from it.

*Your result:* three photos and three sentences.

::: {.check}
A good answer looks like: "Wide: the bottle is on a desk in a classroom
(where). Medium: the bottle and my hand that opens it (what happens).
Close-up: the label with the name (a detail)." Check: the object gets
bigger from photo to photo.
:::
:::

## 5.3 Where does the eye go? Composition

Nour rows to the right. In the first draft, the artist put her at the right
edge of the frame: the boat seems to hit the border. Moving her to the left
gives the player room to look where she goes (@fig-thirds).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 5.3 — Rule of thirds and lead room"}
**Composition** is the way things are placed in the frame. The **rule of
thirds**: two lines across and two lines down split the frame into thirds.
The main subject goes on a line, or where two lines meet. **Lead room** is
empty space in front of a character, where it looks or moves.
:::

![On the left third, Nour has lead room; at the right edge, she has none.](images/thirds.png){#fig-thirds width=96%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 5.3 — Placing Nour"}
The frame is 9 units wide, so the thirds lines are at 3 and 6.

1. Nour rows to the right, so she goes on the **left** line, at 3.
2. The 6 units in front of her are lead room: the player looks there.
3. On the roof, Salma looks to the left, so she goes on the **right**
   line, at 6.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Putting every subject in the exact centre. A centred subject looks still
and leaves no room for movement. Use a thirds line, with lead room in
front.
:::

{{< sim file="sims/frame-lab.html" poster="sims/frame-lab.png" title="Frame Lab: shot size and composition with a camera" height="660" >}}

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Thirds on your phone"}
Turn on the grid of your phone camera (Android: camera settings › Grid
lines; iPhone: Settings › Camera › Grid), or use **Frame Lab** above.

1. Take a photo of a toy or a person that looks to one side. Put it on a
   thirds line, with lead room in front.
2. Take a second photo with the subject at the edge, looking out of the
   frame. Which one feels better? Why?

*Your result:* two photos and one sentence.

::: {.check}
A good answer: "The first photo feels better. The toy is on the left line
and looks right, into the empty space. In the second photo it looks out of
the frame, and the picture feels cut off."
:::
:::

## 5.4 From the scene to the panels: beats and flow

How many panels does a scene need? Not one per sentence. A new **beat**
starts when something changes: a new **place**, a new **action**, a new
**speaker** or a new **feeling**. Each beat gets at least one panel
(@fig-beats).

![From the script to beats to panels.](images/scene-beats.png){#fig-beats width=96%}

The panels are numbered and follow the story: often the place first, then
the action, then the feeling. Arrows show each movement. A movement keeps
its **screen direction** from panel to panel: if Nour rows from left to
right in panel 2, she rows from left to right in panel 4 too. If the
direction flips, the player thinks she turned back.

::: {.callout-note title="Example 5.4 — The beats of the opening"}
1. "EXT. FLOODED STREET – DUSK": a new place. Panel 1, wide.
2. "Nour jumps into the boat": a new action. Panel 2, medium.
3. "NOUR: Hold on, everyone.": a new speaker. Panel 3, close-up.
4. "She rows to the roof": a new action. Panel 4, medium, left to right as
   in panel 2.
5. "SALMA: I won't leave without my cat.": a new speaker and a feeling.
   Panel 5, close-up.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Drawing one panel for every sentence. Two sentences of the same speaker,
with the same feeling, are one beat and one panel.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Beats of a short scene"}
Read the scene: "INT. SALMA'S KITCHEN – NIGHT. Water comes under the door.
Salma lifts the cat onto the table. SALMA: Stay here, Pasha."

1. Mark the beats, and write what changes in each one.
2. Write the shot size of each beat.

*Your result:* a list of beats with a change and a shot size each.

::: {.check}
Beat 1: the kitchen and the water under the door (a new place): wide. Beat
2: Salma lifts the cat (a new action): medium. Beat 3: "Stay here, Pasha."
(a new speaker, a feeling): close-up. Three beats, three panels.
:::
:::

## Case study: storyboarding Rooftop Rescue

*Night Owl Games* storyboards the opening of *Rooftop Rescue*. The beats
are: the flooded street at dusk; Nour jumps into the boat and rows towards
the roof; Nour says "Hold on, everyone. I'm coming."; Nour rows on; on the
roof Salma says "I won't leave without my cat." Nour rows from left to
right in every panel. The board must show the place first, the actions in
medium shots, and the feelings in close-ups. In the mini-game below you
call the shot for each panel.

{{< sim file="sims/shot-caller.html" poster="sims/shot-caller.png" title="Shot Caller: choose the shot for each panel" kind="game" height="700" >}}

## Further reading

Schell, *The Art of Game Design*, 3rd ed., the chapters on story and on
indirect control (how the camera and the frame guide the player). Free
storyboard templates (16:9 frames with caption lines) can be printed from
the web.

## Exercises

1. What is a storyboard? Why does a team draw one before it builds a scene?
2. What does the caption of a panel give?
3. Which shot size shows where a scene happens?
4. Which shot size do you use for a character's fear? Why?
5. What does a low camera angle say about a character?
6. What is the rule of thirds?
7. A character walks to the left. On which thirds line do you place it, and
   why?
8. When does a new beat start?
9. Panel 2 shows a car driving left to right; panel 3 shows it driving
   right to left. What does the player think?
10. *Rooftop Rescue*: write the shot size of the four beats: the street;
    Nour rows; Nour's line; Salma's line.

## Answers to the exercises

::: {.answers}
1. A series of simple drawings that shows shot by shot what the camera shows; a drawing is cheap to change, a built shot is not.
2. The shot size, the action or the line, the sound and the time.
3. The wide (establishing) shot.
4. A close-up: the face shows the feeling.
5. The character looks big and strong.
6. Two lines across and two down split the frame into thirds; the subject goes on a line or where two lines meet.
7. On the right line, so that the lead room is on the left, in front of it.
8. When the place, the action, the speaker or the feeling changes.
9. That the car turned back: the screen direction flipped.
10. Wide; medium; close-up of Nour; close-up of Salma.
:::
